speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am very grateful indeed to my colleague for providing me with this information for, contrary to some of my friends in the opposition, I for one like to learn about things. So I thank him and tell him that I shall remember the lesson for a long time.
Mr. Chairman, in my opinion, and in the opinion of many, the bill under consideration comes a little late maybe since of course the parliamentary procedure must be followed. The hon. member who spoke just before me, said it took us nine months. Well, it takes nine months to give birth to a healthy child and you cannot expect it to be a premature baby. However, this is a good bill. It can be improved upon whenever new circumstances warrant it and new depressed areas appear.
The official opposition complained that the minister was given too much power and I heard others from that side say that the minister had probably not enough power to face all the needs of the provinces or of those underdeveloped areas of Canada.
There were even some to say that the minister was a "pocket C. D. Howe". On the contrary, I believe the minister needs the utmost power to find the answers to what the opposition has been complaining about for nine months, namely that there is still too much poverty in Canada and too much unemployment, that the economy in Canada is at a standstill. Of course this is not something special to Canada. Everybody knows that it is a plague that affects all of mankind.
We were glad to read in the newspapers, yesterday or the day before, that Canada is the third most successful country in the world, after Western Germany and Holland, in its fight against inflation.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, the minister must have extensive enough powers to be able to synchronize the efforts of all the departments, so that we do not run into red tape when the time comes to pass fundamental measures. That red tape requires that in addition to the minister and the deputy minister, civil servants, technocrats, task forces, members, agencies representing the regional promotion
DEBATES	6927
Government Organization organizations, all must intervene, in addition to which the consent of the provinces must be obtained. In fact, there is no end to it. The minister must therefore be granted powers.
I have absolutely no objection to his resembling the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe who was one of the most active advocates of economic promotion we have known in a century. I am sure history will judge him differently from the way the opposition did at the time when he fought political battles here. One can pass judgment by looking at the results of his work here, because he was a realist. I only hope that the new minister of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion will produce as much as the Right Hon. C. D. Howe.
Mr. Chairman, it is high time for us to be realists, to keep both feet on the ground. It is high time to stop discussing such nebulous matters as the constitution for instance.
I am sure that the Newfoundland fishermen who are now going through a critical period are far less interested in the constitution than they are in knowing what they will get next week for their take.
I am sure also that the unemployed of Ste-Rose-du-Degele or St-Etienne-des-Gres are far less interested in knowing whether the constitution will eventually be revised than in getting a job as soon as possible that they might earn a living.
That is why I am of those who rejoice in the introduction of this bill which will allow a minister to synchronize the efforts of all his colleagues and deal with regional economic disparities in this country to fight poverty so that we might all live in honest affluence.
Mr. Chairman, I say again it is time to stop dreaming and waiting for Santa Claus to bring something every year.
I heard fantastic things in this house, in the last few weeks. For instance, some want everyone to live well on free government allowances of a $100 a month, and at the same time, they say that we should not create too many industries which would ruin other industries. All the same, we must be realistic if we want Canadians to earn a living. Indeed, we must give them an opportunity to support themselves and allow financiers to make profits they will re-invest in the economy thus creating employment for workers who otherwise would depend on the state and would increase the financial burdens of government.
March 20, 1969

Government Organization
Mr. Chairman, some fundamental things must be pointed out when speaking about economic development particularly in less favored sectors. So, I would like to make some remarks to the minister.
We would be in a much better position, Mr. Chairman, to promote a strong and lasting economic expansion if, instead of exporting our natural resources to the United States at ridiculous prices, we could have them processed here, by our people and sell the products to other countries, so that Canadians could really benefit from the resources nature has given them.
I am one of those who are shocked to see in front of the city of Trois-Rivieres that I represent, large boats so heavily loaded that each year, the St. Lawrence must be dredged to let them bring, as far as the Great Lakes, to American harbors, our iron ore that the United States will refine, make into tools or machines that they will sell back to us at high prices, with the result that the Americans make profits with the natural resources that we sold them, often for very little.
I do not want to blame the government for this situation, because I know it has been going on for many years. I know who is most responsible and I wonder if the federal government could not, after having concluded an agreement with the provinces, legislate so that our natural resources would be processed here, in the best interests of ah Canadians.
I shall quote as an example, someone who is no more, but who earned himself much fame in Canadian politics, the Hon. Alexandre Taschereau. He said once to American capitalists: If you wish to develop our forest resources, you should build mills and manufacture paper here. As far as my area is concerned, this has always ensured our prosperity. I feel that under a well-planned economic development program, we should try to take steps in order to compel foreigners to process our natural resources' here.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make another suggestion which I think is constructive and realistic. It would be that foreign companies, either British, French or American, which come here to get into business and make profits-I am thinking especially of insurance and finance companies whose headquarters are in Canada-should be compelled, under the law, to invest a considerable proportion of their profits in Canadian industry, so that Canadians may take advantage of that money which was made here, and to prevent it from being directly or indirectly transferred abroad.

I was pleased to note in the bill under consideration, that there would be some cooperation among provinces, municipalities and all organizations concerned.
I should like to plead particularly in favour of municipalities which, in most cases, are treated like poor relatives, when negotiations are under way between the federal and provincial governments.
I would like to plead in favour of regional organizations set up by municipalities which to do so need the assistance of the federal and provincial governments.
Planning bodies, which my colleagues from Timiscouata (Mr. Gendron) referred to a while ago, and economic promotion organizations are used at times to diagnose the problems which business concerns may run into and to find some solutions.
Should the federal government be willing, in conjunction with provincial governments, to help finance such organizations whose members work benevolently and which urgently need experts, the problem of regional disparities could be solved. I should like to quote the case of La Mauricie which brings together some 85 municipalities forming a geographical entity different from the neighbouring regions. Now, the needs of these municipalities are quite alike. They have wanted for many years to set up a dynamic organization but they are unable to do so by their own means .
I recently learned through newspapers- that the Quebec government was expecting a burst of economic expansion which will permit it to invest some $40 million. This is a rather important amount of money for the province. As for the department it intends to invest about $30 million.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
I hope that the two governments in question will help these regional organizations establish specialized offices. These will not only serve to create new enterprises but will permit the old ones to evade difficulties, to find new markets, to develop their operations and, in case of need, to encourage people from the region to invest in the industry and contribute to the economy's revival.
Mr. Chairman, there is another factor upon which I feel I have to dwell, at the risk of being considered a heretic or a babbler.
In fact, I am convinced that governments should legislate on the right to strike which has become a curse and which indirectly
March 20, 1969	COMMONS
undoes governments' efforts to ensure the prosperity of the country.
These days, the right to strike is shamefully misused and most union members have had enough of those recurrent strikes which in the end only increase inflation, add to the worker's burden and make matters worse.
For example, these last few days it was announced that in February alone, 137,070 work-days were lost in the country, for a loss of $2,193,120.
While we are trying to stimulate the economy, there are union leaders without any sense of responsibility who urge workers to strike, get them in debt, and moreover contribute to ruin some businesses.
I could name sax businesses that had to close their doors and two or three others that will have to do the same soon because of unfair strikes.
That is reminiscent of the Middle Ages, and governments should legislate in order to correct that situation.
I could quote testimony of union leaders, who are not just anybody, and who state vigorously that it is time that governments give the workers the machinery needed to settle their disputes without having every time to resort to strike action, to run the risk of jeopardizing the economy of the country and to solve their problems at the expense of the community.
Such little time as I have left does not allow me to elaborate on the legislative priorities that should be established. In any case, others have studied this matter more thoroughly than I have. Legislation should be passed to reduce the number of strikes. Strikes contribute to economic ruin and most union members are fed up with them. After all, they only help to increase the prestige of some labour leaders.
I apologize if my remarks should reflect on the minister, who was active in labour movements in the past, but I know that the special grace pertaining to his function that inspires him today will make him understand things that the grace provided him in his former activity would not allow him to understand then. My charge is constructive, however.
Mr. Chairman, I also wish to speak on another problem. The minister might tell me whether this legislation could solve it.
I know of a French Canadian industry that manufactures snowmobiles, or skidoos, that

Government Organization settled in a rural area represented by a member of the Ralliement Creditiste, and which employs some 300 workers. That industry has been in operation for about four years. It sells 75 per cent of its production to the United States and, being short of capital funds- since it was established with capital invested by farmers and workers1-it has been receiving attractive offers from American financiers. It might soon be sold to some American people.
Therefore, I urge the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) to try and do something and I hope that the act provides some arrangements in favour of such profitable enterprises to keep them in Canadian hands and prevent them from falling into foreign hands, American or others. We should not forget that they have been built at the cost of great sacrifices.
Mr. Chairman, mention was made a while ago of industries that can contribute to regional economic expansion. Among them we find tourism. However, there is always one point that causes difficulties, at least in my province. I mean the constitutional question. Some people are haunted by the constitutional question. Their disease is incurable-

subsubtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND FORESTRY, AND OTHER NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, one
minister and one department to bring together all the federal economic assistance programs for a concerted attack on regional disparity may be all right in theory, but if the
March 20, 1969

Government Organization motivation of the minister and the department is wrong it could result in making a bad situation worse. There will be little hope for success if this newly created instrument is used in the manner that the minister's recent statement indicated it will be used, or if it is employed according to the prevailing philosophy and methods of the government.
Once more, as demonstrated time and time again, we see the trend to centralization and bigness. This government worships at the shrine of bigness-big government, big business, big bureaucracy and big concentrations of votes' such as we find in the metropolitan areas from coast to coast. In its thinking, its planning, in its legislation and in its actions, we have been shown the obsession of this government with figures and theory to the exclusion of the human factor.
In this legislation, as in most of the other measures introduced by the present administration, there appears to be a total absence of human feeling. Individual Canadians rank no higher than so many digits in an economic statistical table. I believe it is time that we, as a nation, stopped catering to bigness. I believe it is time to declare a moratorium on bigness. Let us give some attention and concern to the small things and to the little people of this country. Every day, and more and more, we see evidence of the fact that the individual is rapidly losing his identity and his place in society, his rights. Perhaps this is why we live in a society of dissent, of disorder, of destruction.
Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, this legislation and this portfolio carry with them the absence of humanity, unless we can convince the minister to redirect the attention of the government to the individual and the small masses, those unfortunates who are unable to present their cases, the small farmers, the Indians, the Metis, the Eskimos and the low income family men. We seem to be dominated by computers, figures, percentages, dollars and per capita formulae.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
I hope to see some direction in relieving the rurally depressed areas of Canada. What about the fisherman, the farmer, or the small business firms, all of whom are in a desperate position because of lack of markets for fish and grain. The result is they have low incomes while inflation and high living costs continue. If some direction is not given to provide alternative means for these people to secure a living our situation in the cities will

only become worse. I think it is common sense to assume that unemployment is not solved in the rural areas by directing it to the cities.
The minister has already mentioned specific programs for a number of eastern cities. If all the effort of this department is to be placed on the centres of large population then I say, God help Canada's rural areas and her slow growth centres of low population which represent 90 per cent of this country's land area. What about these thousands of people who are in between? I would hope they would not be written off like the wheat producers of western Canada.
Are all Canadians who do not wish to live in large urban areas now to be labelled "expendable"? It is high time we took a long, close look at this bigness1 that seems to be the governing factor in this government's thinking. Bigness in so far as cities in this country are concerned breeds most of the major problems which face us as a nation. It not only breeds but multiplies them. Where is housing most inadequate and the most pressing problem? It is in the large cities. Where is1 pollution the worst? In and adjacent to the big cities. Where is transportation the most serious problem? In and around the big cities. Where is crime at its1 worst? In the large cities. Where is the cost of living the highest and the quality of life lowest? In the large metropolitan centres. This is inexcusable in a country like Canada where space is one of our outstanding national assets and features. There may be some excuse for urban problems in small European countries; there can be none in Canada. Yet, the government apparently plans to devote the bulk of its attention and public funds to these very same monstrosities.
I believe the whole direction and emphasis in respect of the work of this' new department is wrong and should be corrected in terms of its directive. I believe we should be concentrating on building and developing the rural areas and small population centres. We should be attempting to give all Canadians a fair share of national funds and national effort rather than allowing the already big cities to grow fatter and hog the lion's share of our tax dollars and government effort. In my view, this is- the only way we can hope to improve the essential quality of Canadian life. This is the only way we can answer some of our most pressing problems. It is the only way we can provide equal opportunity for all Canadians from sea to sea, as the minister pointed out in his opening remarks.
March 20, 1969

I suggest that the aid programs and all the skilled assistance should be devoted to encouraging small and middle businesses to establish and prosper in areas where that sort of industrial and commercial endeavour is needed. Let us stop feeding the large corporations and business institutions at the public trough. It is the towns and small cities of Canada which need this aid. They will most richly repay any effort put forward in respect of this type of development.
There is also a national problem of tremendous potential and great urgency facing us today which might be alleviated by application of regional economic development programs. I am speaking now of the problem of bringing our Indian, Metis and Eskimo peoples fully into the social and economic life of this nation. In the Globe and Mail of March 6 there was a story from Regina to the effect that the government of Saskatchewan is setting up a new department of government to deal with this very problem. During the debate it was described by Premier Thatcher as a time bomb with the fuse getting ever shorter, a problem that threatens to become a major social disaster.
The story noted that one of the main aspects of the problem is to find permanent employment for Indian people. Some are reluctant to leave home to obtain work elsewhere, while others take work only to leave it shortly afterward because housing away from their own areas is difficult to procure. In my riding there are a number of Indian Canadians. I speak about the Saddle Lake band'. Just over a year ago the Department of Forestry and Rural Development, working in conjunction with the provincial government and the Saddle Lake band council, undertook to clear and develop 15,000 acres of prime, arable land for the production of crops. To date 3,000 acres are ready for use with an additional 5,000 targeted for next spring. The band members organized1 as a society under the Alberta Societies Act and assumed the responsibility of implementing this most ambitious project aimed at involving a majority of band members. This was the first time a vast field of local employment was made available to the citizens of this area.
The achievement of and the results- from this project were beyond expectation. Besides providing employment for 125 citizens during the clearing operations, it will also provide permanent seasonal employment for 100 citizens who will actually be engaged in the farming operations. This project it
Government Organization demonstrated that these people are willing to accept responsibility and challenge. They are willing to provide for themselves and wish to become self-sustaining citizens. It demonstrated as well that they appreciate receiving a weekly cheque which they have earned. However, this must be done in a manner in which residence can be maintained on the reserve.
What are some of the results of this undertaking? The welfare list diminished to practically nothing when the clearing operation was in progress during the summer months. A saving of 75 per cent in welfare payments was estimated to have been made during the summer. Opportunity was made available for the development of new skills among the residents. Agricultural short courses have followed and there are now 10 young men attending the Vermilion School of Agriculture.
A prefab housing project has been commenced which constructs houses on the reserve. This project is staffed by Indians and the houses are for families on the reserve. The grain produced from the land this year has already been contracted to registered seed houses to be used as seed1 grain. Conceivably, this plan can continue. A livestock enterprise is to follow soon. Discussions are taking place regarding horticulture and poultry operations. Further discussions are taking place regarding the possibility of the shores of Saddle Lake becoming a tourist attraction.
A great step forward has been taken, in an attempt to solve the social economic problems on the reserve. All participants are to be commended, particularly the members of the band, for their imagination, leadership and determination. I repeat, however, that steps must be taken immediately to provide employment for all these people on a permanent basis in order that they may help themselves. I would hope this department and this minister would not overlook the humanistic aspects relating to a group such as this when trying to pacify the masses.
As I said, we have had an encouraging beginning on this reserve. However, living conditions are grossly inadequate. I had an opportunity to conduct my own survey regarding the living conditions in late February. Of some 29 families interviewed, it was discovered all had an inadequate water supply and were either faced with the necessity of hauling drinking water for long distances or utilizing snow or slough water. In this day and age, when many people in Canada enjoy
March 20, 1969

Government Organization one of the highest standards of living in the world, it seems to me it is a grave injustice that there are some who are unable to enjoy even an adequate water supply, one of the basic necessities of life. Similarly, housing is most inadequate. Families of 8 and 10 persons live in one room homes which measure 12 feet by 16 feet. Many of these homes lack any insulation. They are cold in winter and the roofs leak.
I am sure that this department, working in close co-operation with the Indian Affairs branch and the various band councils, together with the many industrial development bodies and chambers of commerce throughout the country, could do much to assist these people in achieving their hopes and aspirations. With the proper leadership and liaison, this department could become the most effective vehicle in Canada, if it considers people to be human beings rather than masses of voters. The native citizens are not desirous of leaving their reservations, homes and families. They are loath to move as a single family unit away from the reservations to a strange environment.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
What could be more simple than to assist in the establishment of light industries, service industries and small commercial enterprises reasonably close to the reservations. In this way, the Indians would not have to leave home, family or reservations and yet would be assured of steady work at reasonable wages. Then, they would be well on the road to full participation in our Canadian national life.
Why must we crowd everything together in a country where fresh air, space and natural beauty are all around us? What excuse is there for the nightmare "megopolis" that is even now being suggested by our planners and experts, an urban monster that will stretch in an unbroken line from Montreal through Toronto to Windsor and Niagara Falls. The amount of money that will be required just to make life in that industrial slum bearable will be a thousand times greater than is required now to make rural Canada prosperous, attractive and a fully producing sector of the national economy.
Unfortunately, the pattern seems to be that when the government offers economic incentives or assistance, the major part of it is gobbled up in fierce competition between our huge metropolitan centres. In my own province of Alberta the competition is so fierce between Edmonton and Calgary in the scramble for even the smallest industry, that the

small city or town is beyond consideration before any opportunity is given to hear its proposals. Big business acts in the same way, crowding out the small operator and forcing him out of business.
It is ironic that there is always lots of money for stone and mortar in the big cities, but never more than a few pennies for building in the small town. It is not enough to say that this is an irreversible economic trend. If we are looking for challenges, surely this is the greatest we can find. This is a way to reverse the trend and make a more natural, more satisfying life possible for our people.
We have recently concluded a debate on the terrible housing crisis in Canada. I listened with interest to the remarks made by members on all sides of the house outlining the lack of accomodation in the cities and the lack of recreational facilities for children to romp and play, as well as the lack of parking facilities. I can only conclude that most of these problems are man-made. Too many of our experts, too many of our planners and too many Ottawa bureaucrats tend to take European and United States experience as gospel. They continually point to the United States for reasons why we in Canada cannot do this or that, to prove that we in Canada are bound by the experience of others and subject to their lead.
Surely, in seeking to fulfil our national destiny we can do better than copy the United States, or anyone else for that matter. There is no reason under the sun why we should be bound by what has happened to others or by what others are doing in seeking to develop our own separate and distinctive national life. Let us innovate, not duplicate. We are different in history, in our economy and, above all, in our geography. Let us use the advantages these differences confer upon us. Let us do our own "thing" regardlessi of others. We have the land, we have the distribution of population, and we have the economic set up to make an ideal mixture of rural and urban life. All we have to do is to make up our minds to undertake the job.
I have serious misgivings about the concept of bigness in this country. I wonder where it may lead us if the trend is not averted. This is the challenge to the minister of this new department. I hope he will give consideration to some of the points which I have raised. I hope also that his department will provide the necessary leadership and incentives to give all Canadians in rural and urban areas the opportunity to share in the wealth of Canada, the results of which will make this
March 20, 19G9	COMMONS
country a healthier and happier nation for all Canadians from sea to sea.

speechtext:
It is with pleasure, Mr. Chairman, that I participate in this debate. In fact Bill C-173 is made up of several clauses and it is intended to establish a Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
DEBATES	6933
Government Organization
Mr. Chairman, it is the government's responsibility to exercise its powers in the best interests of the people.
This bill includes several good points, but the Minister will not be able to realize some of them because the Canadian sources of capital supplies will not be adequate and this will be the case for capital investments by foreign countries. This bill does not provide for the creation, by the government, of adequate capital resources to effect what is physically possible and to realize what is possible and feasible from the physical but not from the financial viewpoint. This is what the Minister will come up against.
The Minister is given a spring with only a trickle of water. He is granted a certain amount of money and when that amount is spent, the spring will have dried up.
The underdeveloped regions will remain underdeveloped because the means of development will be missing and because the spring will have been diverted from its course. Whatever little capital is left will be taken away for other purposes, as well as the few drops from the stream; this will greatly reduce the activity in the economic field.
The field of activities devolved to the Minister is the development of economically weak regions in Canada and goodness knows there is quite a bit of them.
I would like to tell him about my region, one of the first regions to be settled in Canada. At one time, it was prosperous; today, it is going bankrupt, and people are leaving in droves. What is the cause of such a situation? The present system.
It is a fact that the old political parties, the key administrators, the key economists who know it all, who have all the answers but who solve nothing, who drive us deeper into debt, are the ones to blame. The minister will not be able to achieve any economic regional development without getting us deeper into debt.
Some 410 million dollars worth of bonds have matured. That is an old debt, and we are not told when it was incurred nor whether those bonds were sold. We are told that they are payable and redeemable now and that we do not have the money for this purpose. More money must be borrowed at the new interest rate and this leads to new taxes and to new problems for the population and for the regions that are already overburdened, overtaxed and that will continue to be taxed in order to protect capital and bonds which we will have to pay for until Doomsday. We pay
March 20, 1969

Government Organization the interest, so those bonds could already have been reimbursed three or four times.
This bill does not make any provision whatever to deal with this problem. That is where the minister will find himself in hot water. That will hinder his efforts and his work. Apparently, he is in good health and his intentions are of the best. We have confidence in him, we know that he can do his job and this pleases us. We admire his ability but we know that he will find himself in conflict with financial interests. However, no member of the other parties wishes to solve the financial problem.
It seems all members favour this kind of debenture redemption. Some of them mature every two or three months. The increase of capital and of interests contribute to widen the gap between the wealthy and the poor. The minister wants to correct this situation. If this situation is to be corrected the other situation must also be corrected. However, the government does not intend to do so.
Those great economists of ours are not in favour of this. Since they have invested capital in debentures, they think it is a splendid idea to increase the interest rate and to create everlasting debts, while they may lead the life of Riley. Once those debentures have been issued by those institutions, interest has to be paid for 30, 40, 50 years, practically forever. Those debentures bring high profits and are renewed periodically at a higher and higher interest rate, and this brings about our economic stagnation. I do not think there are two members on the government side who could prove me wrong. Not one of them has ever stood up and denounced this system.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND FORESTRY. AND OTHER NEW DEPARTMENTS
speechtext: Order. I shall ask the hon. member to address himself to the Bill before us. Plants with 250 employees, and others with 50 or 60 employees, are closing down. For ininstance, the town of Scotstown, formerly had a population of 5,000 people of which 350 worked for a local industry which went out of business about ten years ago. Today the population has dwindled to 1,500; they have been left with debts of all kinds: municipal, school, vestry-board, etc. The people are head over heels in debt because the town at one time was prosperous but has now become rundown, a dead town, a ghost-town where properties that used to be worth $25,000 are now up for sale for $2,000 and $3,000. The situation is sad indeed now. That is why I ask the minister to include our area amongst the designated areas. Ours is one of the oldest areas and also one of the less prosperous, and the most affected in the whole of Canada. It is located in the eastern townships, and yet I know other areas in Canada which are like mine.

To operate the economy of a country, Mr. Chairman, you need resources.
March 20, 1969	COMMONS
If we lack money at all times, how can we expect the economy to operate properly? If you drive out in your car and then going up the hill you run out of gas, you have to get out and walk perhaps ten miles to get gas, which is hardly advantageous.
This is what happens in our present economic system. The economic, financial machine lacks the necessary fuel to make the engine run.
The purpose of the bill under consideration is to establish various industries. The purpose of the industry is to produce as much as possible with the least possible effort and not to create manpower. Today the industry wants to use to a maximum scientific, technical and mechanical means but this is not a way to create jobs. The needs of the people remain unfulfilled. It is not necessary to administer in terms of machinery and science but rather in terms of the human person who has needs within the family.
Therefore, this bill should provide a plan which would guarantee an income to every citizen who has the right to live. Canada produces enough to feed five times as many people as we have now. What every citizen needs then is a guaranteed income and an adequate purchasing power to keep industry going. They want to create industries but the purpose of this bill is to get our products to markets abroad. We are going to sell the best of what we have and we Canadians, who are not very wise, will content ourselves with what remains. Such is the purpose of the bill under consideration now.
Let the government promote the investment of foreign capital in our country, yes. We want some of that capital, but it will never contribute to the development of Canada, it will never make it possible for Canadians to own their own land, homes, industries, natural resources, in brief, they will always be nothing but tenants.
But Mr. Chairman, I should like to tell the minister that if foreign capital is to establish itself in Canada, I would like to know why our national agency should not issue the same credits on the same guarantees.
Such is, Mr. Chairman, one of the solutions we could offer. If the minister had opened his eyes a little more, he could have offered a solution similar to that provided in the bill. We could then find sources of supply and say one of these days that Canadians can own something, that they will not always be only drawers of water.

Mr. Chairman, I would have much to say on this bill but I would rather ask the minister what he intends to do to develop that tremendous economic activity. Where will he get the money to so? Will it take fifty, a hundred or two hundred years to materialize? It has been said that about $130 million were made available to the minister to get that agency going. But it is merely a drop in the ocean. We will not go far with $130 million far all Canada. The minister said that everything has to be done, and that there were lots of fields where development could take place.
We hear about the development of the tourist industry, and of all kinds of things but the tourist industry is not a solution to all our ills, to all our problems.
It may be an answer though I cannot see why, in order to attract tourists, one should borrow money at a 10 per cent rate of interest then pay it back practically every eight years in the form of interests, thus remaining indefinitely in debt and paying higher taxes.
If the tourist industry were run that way, we would get the same results as in all the other sectors of our economy.
We have to finance regional disparities. If we prove unable to appropriately combine public and private investments, we are doomed to failure. In fact, we go on borrowing capital at extravagant rates and we strangle the taxpayers for the sake of development.
A moment ago, the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Gendron) told us that the Creditistes suggest all kinds of answers and go on repeating over and over again that once war is declared everything becomes possible. He added that we forget to say that you then have to get indebted, to borrow money at frightful rates of interests1 which strangle the people.
As for those bonds, worth $410 million, they are war bonds, I believe. They are always renewable at current rates.
Mr. Chairman, we are not advocating war; we just say that war should not be waged for the sake of profit. Wars should be waged with capital hearing interest according to management costs only. The same should apply to the development of the public sector and the Canadian economy.
The new department should not be concerned with making money. Then, Mr. Chairman, we could get out of the ditch and do
March 20, 1969

Government Organization something to improve and balance our economy. The more we play with the present systems, and the more we set up bodies such as this one, the more we upset our economy. We shall never be able to balance it with the means available to us now. Those means are old-fashioned, obsolete; they are applied in every country and always lead to the same results, that is bankruptcy, new increases in taxes. They lead to disaster because the people become discouraged, because the workers no longer wants to work, their tax burden being too heavy.
We can increase the production of the country, by using Canadian capital with Canadian guarantees, the same that we give abroad. That is how we can again become the owners of our heritage, of our industries. At the present time, we can hardly operate our industries, especially the small ones. There are awful problems. Two or three accountants are needed just to keep books for the government. And the government does not pay for that.
In our economic system, the citizens are unable to pay because their taxes are too high.

Mr. Chairman, I am still under the shock of my hon. friend's speech. I do not know whether to rejoice at his eloquence or shudder at the gloomy picture he has conjured up for us.
March 20, 1969

In any case, I feel I represent a "have-not" area in many ways, but rich nevertheless in the burning desire of my fellow-citizens to co-operate with the government in finding permanent solutions to their problems.
I am happy to see that the hon. minister has been given the responsibility of the new Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
I believe he is highly qualified for the job and I want to tell him at this point that he can count on my full support and co-operation. As ill-luck would have it, I did not get to hear the minister's speech this afternoon, but I will make it a point to read his remarks in tomorrow's Hansard.
Mr. Chairman, I am not an expert in matters of regional economic expansion, yet I would like to make some comments on the subject.
I am not pessimistic by nature either, and moreover I am very patient when long term solutions have to be found in order to settle, if not for ever, at least for some time, our problems of regional disparities.
When one speaks of the plans of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, one thinks at once of the confrontation of ideologies that might occur between the federal government, on the one hand, and regional governments or a provincial government, on the other hand.
I submit that a conflict may arise in some cases between the priority needs of a given province and the solutions proposed by the federal government in order to help a province put its economy back on its feet.
I do not know who will have a right of priority in both cases but I am convinced that we must co-operate with the utmost common sense. As for me, I am satisfied with the co-operation from the Atlantic provinces in connection with the proposals made by the federal government so far.
However, one point worries me. To work out those plans, federal officials will be used and at times I doubt that some of them understand our regional problems. As a matter of principle, I find it hard to admit that someone who has always lived in the central provinces, who has studied there, who has found his theories there, may find possible solutions to problems of regional disparities and bring a valuable contribution to the solution of regional problems. However, I give them the benefit of the doubt.
But, in my opinion, what is essential is that governments make allowances for ideas and proposals from the people we want to help.

EXTERNAL AID-PROVISION OF FOOD THROUGH TRANSFER OF ARMAMENT FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago on orders of the day I sought to raise the following question:
Is consideration being given to the suggestion of a national body, the Canadian Catholic Conference, that 10 per cent of Canada's armaments expenditures be spent instead on such peace efforts as the provision of food for under-developed countries?
At that time Mr. Speaker ruled the question out of order and I have taken the opportunity tonight to try to raise it again. In the few moments at my disposal, I wish to put some statistics on the record in support of the basis for the question.
As we know, Mr. Speaker, the great producing powers of the world are teetering on a balance of terror with regard to defence expenditures, without very much hope that present vast expenditures on mutual destruction can be reduced. According to the United
March 20, 1969

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Nations Arms Control and Disarmament Agency the current cost to the world of armaments is $182 billion a year. The United States alone spends $80 billion every 12 months. Between NATO and the Warsaw Pact countries 90 per cent of the world's armament expenditures is incurred.
The total arms bill of the world is equal to three times the world's spending on public health, and is 40 per cent more than the world's spending on education. It represents $53 for every man, woman and child in the world and, as hon. members well realize, in some countries $53 is often the difference between life and death.
As pointed out in the letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) from the Canadian Catholic Conference:
Some members oi your government have begun to compare Canada's high level oi defence expenditures to the relatively low level of foreign assistance. This ratio is now nearly six to one ... One interesting suggestion, for example, proposed that for a start Canada might transfer 10 per cent from her defence budget to development projects.
In my opinion, no country in the world from the point of view of history, geography and economics is more favourably situated than Canada to give leadership to the world on this serious issue of armaments as against peace expenditures. A 10 per cent reduction would mean very little difference in Canada's defence strength in this nuclear age, but it would mean a great deal of difference in the respect of the world for Canada 'and the defence of the world itself, because this would be constructive spending for peace, spending on food and medicine for other countries1. I urge that the government give serious consideration to this 10 per cent proposal, 10 per cent less for defence in the armements sense, and 10 per cent more for peace in the sense of spending to help the hungry and the sick people of other countries.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. Walker (Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: EXTERNAL AID-PROVISION OF FOOD THROUGH TRANSFER OF ARMAMENT FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no way, of course, that I can undertake to the house that this government intends to transfer any specific part of its revenues from one task to another. Nor, I should say, is there necessarily anything meaningful about statistical comparisons. There are any number of methods of computing defence budgets just as there are a number of ways of calculating sums spent on economic assistance programs. Even the technique employed by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development offers suitable scope for variation among reporting countries.

I welcome the opportunity, however, to reaffirm to the house the conviction of the government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that one of the foremost problems in the world today is that of the spread of economic standards as between the rich nations and the poor nations. One of the priorities of this government, and the governments of all of the industrial nations of the earth, must be the raising of the standard of living of the two thirds of the human race who live in conditions of abject poverty. Should the expectations of the persons of the so-called "third world" not be fulfilled, then the latter part of this century is likely to be a most unsettled one.
The government is continuing and indeed increasing its participation in the Colombo Plan, and in a variety of other assistance programs of which the house is aware. The Government is as well taking a serious interest in the affairs of U.N.C.T.A.D., United Nations Conference on Trade and Development, in the belief that the long range solution to the economic difficulties of all nations, both developed and developing, is a world in which international trade plays a major role. Only when the developing countries are able to sell their goods abroad will their economies attain the self-generating stage.
In conclusion, may I say that the aim of Canada's economic assistance programs is to assist the developing countries to achieve a high degree of economic independence. They are not intended as a mere palliative or food give-away program. We help in these ways in emergencies, but much prefer to assist the countries to grow their own food, manufacture their own goods and harness their own resources. This is our aim and is one which I am sure all Canadians support.

Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I opened the can of worms with regard to lumber prices. Regrettably, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) was the only appropriate minister in the house at the time to which to pop the question. I had actually intended to direct the question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) in his capacity as minister primarily concerned with housing. I see that, unfortunately, the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has taken the ball back in this regard. I am sorry to have imposed' on either him or his minister in this regard because I do not really believe there is any
March 20, 19G9

reason to speculate that activities in this market area should be subjected to scrutiny by the combines investigation branch.
The fact remains, however, that price changes in the lumber industry over the past year or over the past few months have been little short of monumental. The figures which I shall quote here have been taken from actual invoices which I have obtained from contractors in Calgary whom I believe to be in a position of driving the best bargain that is available in this particular market. I shall not cite all these prices by any means. I believe a few will illustrate my point. Fir lumber in the dimensions of 2 inches by 4 inches by 16 feet was invoiced on February 20, 1968 at $124.75 a thousand board feet. On March 12, 1969 it was invoiced at $177. This is an increase of 41.8 per cent. Then, 2 inch by 6 inch by 14 foot fir was invoiced on March 27, 1968 at $118 a thousand board feet. On February 24 it was selling at $175 a thousand. This is an increase of 48.4 per cent. Fir sheathing, which is used on the sides of a house, increased in price over 20 per cent between August 1968 and March 1969. Some specific items have increased in amounts over 100 per cent. For example, grade 2 shingles have increased 135 per cent over what they were a year ago. There are many other examples.
These examples are typical of what seems to have occurred in the industry. I might quote directly from a letter from a building supply company in Calgary to its customers. Usually, they send out price lists but recently they have been sending out the following notice:
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Due to present shortages and the price fluctuation of lumber and plywood, which may continue for some time, we are unable to furnish you with our normal price list.
However, we will be pleased to quote prices for immediate delivery from our stocks on hand.
The situation in the industry is little short of disastrous from the housing point of view, and certainly it is undermining the entire construction industry. The price changes in the last year have been such that there has been an increase of about $800 to $1,000 on the cost of a $20,000 house.
The feelings of the home buyer and of the contractor are not particularly alleviated by the following information published in the Financial Times issue of March 10, 1969:
The forest products companies, particularly the west coast operators, had a bountiful fourth quarter
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
with profit increases averaging 61 per cent following a decline of 32 per cent in the previous nine months.
The whole problem is one that is really continental or world wide. I think it is attributable to the pressures of the export market. The fact is that 75 per cent of our lumber is exported from Vancouver market and 25 per cent is used domestically. Supplies have been far outstripped by demand. It is a very serious matter. As a matter of fact, yesterday the housing subcommittee of the senate committee on banking and finance in the United States, under Senator Sparkman of Alabama, commenced sittings on the lumber situation as a result of requests made by the National Association of Homebuilders.
We are in a steadily worsening crisis with regard to the prices and supply of forest products. This is having a disastrous inflationary effect on the stability of the construction industry generally. The pain is not assuaged by the knowledge that profits in the manufacturing segment of this industry have increased greatly, as did those in wholesale distribution.
We have a problem here that is of immediate concern to the nation. We want our export trade,-it is important to us-but there is a recognized crisis in housing. Somehow or other we have to achieve a balance between our export prices on the one hand and the legitimate needs and requirements of the construction industry generally and housing in particular. I respectfully submit that some very top level governmental action is indicated to investigate the current situation.

I appreciate the concern of the hon. member about the recent increased cost of lumber in Canada which apparently is also a problem and a matter of concern in the United States. The report of the task force on housing and urban development evidently contained a statement of the problem of the cost of building materials but it did not comment specifically on the recent increase in the cost of lumber. It appears the increase in lumber prices has occurred especially in the last few months and is evident in more than one province. It should be noted that in the last year or two we have experienced in Canada, as has the United States recently, a
